name: Kaur
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: As far as KL was concerned, the primary stress on a one-syllable basic morpheme was on the vowel of the syllable, the primary stress on a two-syllable basic morpheme was on the final syllable, the primary stress on a three- syllable basic morpheme was on the penultimate syllable, and that on a four-syllable basic morpheme was on the penultimate syllable as well. [...] This study also found shifts in the patterns of stress triggered by the increasing number of syllables as a result of affixation process.
new_statements.citation: Hadi, Wisman, I Wayan Pastika, I Nyoman Suparwa & A.A. Putu Putra. 2012. Phonology of Kaur language in generative theory. e-Journal of Linguistics (Universitas Udayana) 6(1), Januari 2012 (article 13893; PDF dated Feb 2013)
new_statements.locator: §3.5 'Patterns of Stress in KL', printed p. 6 (PDF p. 6 of 15)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (15 pp., text layer, doPDF 2013-02-04). §3.5 "Patterns of Stress in KL" begins on printed p. 6 (= PDF p. 6) and the quoted passage is there word for word, including the odd "three- syllable" spacing: "As far as KL was concerned, the primary stress on a one-syllable basic morpheme was on the vowel of the syllable, the primary stress on a two-syllable basic morpheme was on the final syllable, the primary stress on a three- syllable basic morpheme was on the penultimate syllable, and that on a four-syllable basic morpheme was on the penultimate syllable as well." The closing sentence of the quote ("This study also found shifts in the patterns of stress triggered by the increasing number…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress is predictable from the syllable count of the base: final syllable in disyllabic bases, penultimate syllable in three- and four-syllable bases (monosyllables stressed on their one vowel). The one acoustic example is the four-syllable base kejejambai /kɘɟɘɑmbaɪ/ 'whiskers' with the penult [ɟam] stressed (218 ms vs 151/125 ms for the other syllables). Stress position moves when affixation changes the syllable count.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated as such; the source notes only that stress 'shifts' under affixation as syllable count increases. Note the disyllabic-final vs. longer-penult split is unusual for Malayic and may reflect schwa-repulsion in penults (the example base has schwa in its first two syllables), but the source frames it purely by syllable count.
new_statements.domain_note: Stated for basic morphemes (bases) in isolation; affixed words follow the same count-based placement. Data from six older native-speaker informants in Kaur Regency, collected Aug 2010-Mar 2012; acoustic measurements with SIL Speech Analyzer. This is the published summary of Hadi's 2012 Udayana dissertation, with one worked example; the F1 discussion on p. 6 is internally inconsistent (says stressed-syllable F1 'much higher' while the numbers given are lower), so treat the phonetic support as thin.
new_statements.identity_note: The statement is for the Kaur language as spoken in Kaur Regency, Bengkulu (Hadi's informants; Hadi 2011 mentions speakers in Kaur Selatan, Maje and Nasal districts), which Hadi classifies as a variety of 'Central Malay' — this is kaur1269 [vkk]. McDowell & Anderbeck 2020 treat Kaur as a lect of the HIGHLAND cluster of their BARISAN language (South Barisan Malay) with a southern Bintuhan dialect (Lampung-influenced) and a North Kaur dialect (Besemah-influenced); Hadi does not specify which dialect his informants represent.

sources.locator: §3.5 'Patterns of Stress in KL', printed p. 6 (PDF p. 6 of 15)
sources.note: §3.5 'Patterns of Stress in KL' (p. 6): primary stress on the vowel in monosyllabic bases, on the FINAL syllable in disyllabic bases, on the PENULT in three- and four-syllable bases; one acoustic example kejejambai /kɘɟɘɑmbaɪ/ 'whiskers' with [ɟam] stressed (218 ms); stress shifts when affixation adds syllables.
No phonology section; cites only Ethnologue and McDowell & Anderbeck 2020.

sources.note: Phonotactics (consonant clusters and series) only; no mention of stress or accent.

sources.citation: McDowell, Jonathan & Karl Anderbeck. 2020. The Malay lects of southern Sumatra. JSEALS Special Publication 7. Honolulu: University of Hawai'i Press. 178 pp. hdl:10524/52473
sources.note: Dialect survey; Kaur profile §2 (c. p. 25: two dialects, Bintuhan/south with Lampung influence and North Kaur with Besemah influence; HIGHLAND cluster of BARISAN). Historical-phonology chapter discusses penultimate vowel lowering but contains no statement on word stress for Kaur or any lect.

sources.citation: Hadi, Wisman. 2011. Proses fonologis bahasa Kaur yang dipicu faktor eksternal linguistik. In: Proceedings of the International Seminar 'Language Maintenance and Shift', Diponegoro University, 2 July 2011, pp. 348-352.
sources.note: Externally-triggered (geographic/social) phonological processes; silent on word stress ('tekanan' occurs only as 'tekanan bahasa lain' = pressure from other languages).
